newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Kohl's Indonesia tour fruitful but can't meet Belo.
newsitem.headline: Kohl's Indonesia tour fruitful but can't meet Belo.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl said on Monday his visit to Indonesia was fruitful but the German leader was apparently snubbed by Nobel Peace laureate Bishop Carlos Belo, who did not show up for a meeting he was invited to.

Kohl told reporters he had held meaningful discussions with President Suharto and other officials said that the German delegation accompanying him had signed contracts worth 1.34 billion marks ($855 million) with Indonesian businessmen.
"It was a good meeting," Kohl said. "We have agreed to expand our relationship in all sectors."
He said his talks with Suharto touched on human rights and the troubled territory of East Timor, but did not give details.
But Kohl's visit was marred by the apparent reluctance of East Timorese Bishop Belo to accept an invitation for a meeting.
"I regret it was cancelled," Kohl said, adding that apparently Belo was busy touring East Timor.

Kohl arrived in Jakarta on Saturday for his fourth visit to Indonesia since 1983. He spent a relaxed day fishing in the Java Sea with Indonesian President Suharto on Sunday before the official leg of his visit on Monday.
He leaves for the Philippines on Tuesday morning.
German delegation sources said Kohl had been expected to meet Belo, but the bishop failed to appear at a meeting the chancellor had on Monday afternoon with other Indonesian church leaders.
There was no response from phone calls to Belo's home in the East Timor capital, Dili, or from church aides in the former Portuguese colony.
Indonesian Foreign Minister Ali Alatas told a news briefing Belo might have had previous commitments.
"I heard that Bishop Belo had some other commitments and unfortunately that (meeting) has not taken place yet," he said. "Maybe it will take place before he (Kohl) leaves but I don't know."

Belo was jointly awarded the 1996 Nobel Peace Prize early this month together with self-exiled East Timorese resistance leader Jose Ramos-Horta, who had called on Kohl to raise the East Timor issue with Suharto.
Indonesian troops took over East Timor in December 1975 and Jakarta declared it Indonesia's 27th province the following July in a move the United Nations has refused to recognise.
Indonesia's State Secretary Murdiono told reporters after the meeting between Suharto and Kohl that they had discussed human rights issues.
"The president (Suharto) explained about the implementation of human rights in Indonesia and also about the development in East Timor," Murdiono said.
"The implementation of human rights certainly cannot be separated from the nation's historical values," he added.
But a major focus of the visit was trade and economic ties, with a number of ministers and businessmen accompanying the chancellor.
German Economic Minister Guenter Rexrodt said the visit had produced 25 contracts and memoranda of understanding, including purchase orders and joint venture agreements.
The contracts signed included an agreement by Fried Krupp AG to build a $100 million aromatics plant in Indonesia.
Germany is Indonesia's largest European market with two-way trade estimated at US$4.46 billion in 1995, up 75 percent from 1990.
